12-01.script:
On the first of December in 1955, in Montgomery, Alabama, a seamstress named Rosa Parks was riding home after a long day of work. When the bus driver told her to give up her seat for a white passenger, she quietly said no. Her arrest sparked a bus boycott that lasted more than a year, led by a young preacher named Martin Luther King Jr.

On this day in 1783, a crowd in Paris watched Jacques Charles rise into the sky in the first balloon filled with hydrogen.

In 1959, twelve nations signed the Antarctic Treaty, agreeing that the frozen continent would be kept for peace and science.

And in 1990, deep beneath the English Channel, British and French workers broke through the last wall of chalk and shook hands. For the first time since the Ice Age, Britain was joined to the continent.

Today is World AIDS Day, a day to remember, and to keep caring. Romania celebrates its Great Union Day, and the Indian state of Nagaland the day it was formed in 1963.

events.text: Portugal rises against Spanish rule and restores its independence.
Jacques Charles makes the first flight in a hydrogen balloon.
Ford's moving assembly line begins producing entire cars.
Transylvania unites with Romania.
Nancy Astor takes her seat, the first woman to sit in the British House of Commons.
Rosa Parks refuses to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama.
Twelve nations sign the Antarctic Treaty, reserving the continent for science and peace.
Nagaland becomes the 16th state of India.
The United States holds its first draft lottery since the Second World War.
Workers digging the Channel Tunnel break through between Britain and France.

births.text: Bette Midler, American singer and actress

names: International Day for the Abolition of Slavery
12-02.script:
On the second of December in 1804, in the great cathedral of Notre-Dame in Paris, Napoleon Bonaparte took the crown from the hands of the Pope and placed it on his own head. Exactly one year later, in 1805, he won his most brilliant victory, at Austerlitz.

On this same date in 1942, beneath the stands of a sports field at the University of Chicago, scientists led by Enrico Fermi watched their instruments in silence. For the first time, a nuclear chain reaction sustained itself. A coded message was sent: the Italian navigator has landed in the new world.

In 1971, six emirates on the Arabian Gulf joined together as the United Arab Emirates, and a seventh soon followed. Today they celebrate their National Day.

In 1982, a dentist named Barney Clark became the first person to receive a permanent artificial heart.

Today is the International Day for the Abolition of Slavery. In India, it is National Pollution Control Day, remembering the victims of the Bhopal gas tragedy.

events.text: St Paul's Cathedral in London, rebuilt after the Great Fire, opens for its first service.
Napoleon crowns himself Emperor of the French at Notre-Dame.
Battle of Austerlitz: Napoleon defeats the Russian and Austrian armies.
President James Monroe announces the Monroe Doctrine.
Ford introduces the Model A, successor to the Model T.
Enrico Fermi's team achieves the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction, in Chicago.
The U.S. Senate votes to censure Senator Joseph McCarthy.
The United Arab Emirates is formed.
Barney Clark receives the first permanent artificial heart.
Benazir Bhutto is sworn in as Prime Minister of Pakistan.
Space Shuttle Endeavour launches on a mission to repair the Hubble Space Telescope.
The SOHO observatory is launched to study the Sun.

names: International Day of Persons with Disabilities
12-03.script:
On the third of December in 1967, in a hospital in Cape Town, a surgeon named Christiaan Barnard lifted out a man's failing heart and placed a new one in its place. For the first time, a human heart had been transplanted. The world was astonished.

Twenty-five years later, in 1992, an engineer in England typed two words on a computer and sent them to a mobile phone: Merry Christmas. It was the very first text message.

In 1973, the little probe Pioneer 10 flew past Jupiter, the first visitor from Earth to the giant planet, and sent back pictures of its swirling clouds.

The day also carries great sorrow. In the early hours of this day in 1984, a cloud of poisonous gas leaked from a factory in Bhopal, and thousands of people lost their lives in their sleep.

Today is the International Day of Persons with Disabilities. And born on this day in 1884 was Dr. Rajendra Prasad, the first President of India.

events.text: The French defeat the Austrians at the Battle of Hohenlinden.
Illinois becomes the 21st U.S. state.
Neon lighting is shown to the public for the first time, at the Paris Motor Show.
Tennessee Williams's A Streetcar Named Desire opens on Broadway.
The musical Camelot opens on Broadway.
Christiaan Barnard performs the first human heart transplant, in Cape Town.
The Indo-Pakistani War of 1971 begins.
Pioneer 10 makes the first flyby of Jupiter.
A gas leak at a pesticide plant in Bhopal, India, kills thousands of people.
At the Malta Summit, Bush and Gorbachev signal the end of the Cold War.
The first SMS text message, "Merry Christmas", is sent.

births.text: Samuel Crompton, English inventor of the spinning mule
Rajendra Prasad, first President of India

facts.text: The International Day of Persons with Disabilities was proclaimed by the United Nations in 1992.
Louis Washkansky, the first heart transplant patient, lived for 18 days after his operation.

12-04.script:
On the fourth of December in 1872, sailors on a passing ship spotted a vessel drifting in the Atlantic, its sails half set. They climbed aboard the Mary Celeste and found no one. The cargo was untouched, there was food in the stores, but the crew had vanished. To this day, no one knows exactly what happened.

On this day in 1829, the British governor of Bengal banned the cruel practice of sati, after years of campaigning by the reformer Raja Ram Mohan Roy.

In 1956, four young musicians happened to meet at Sun Studio in Memphis: Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash, Jerry Lee Lewis and Carl Perkins. They sang together around a piano, and the recording became known as the Million Dollar Quartet.

In 1971, the Indian Navy launched a daring night attack on the port of Karachi. India celebrates today as Navy Day.

And in 1996, NASA launched Mars Pathfinder, carrying a little rover called Sojourner.

events.text: Jeremiah Horrocks becomes the first person known to watch a transit of Venus.
The Observer, the world's first Sunday newspaper, is published in London.
The practice of sati is banned in Bengal.
The ship Mary Celeste is found drifting in the Atlantic with no one aboard.
President Woodrow Wilson sails for the Paris Peace Conference.
Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash, Jerry Lee Lewis and Carl Perkins jam together as the Million Dollar Quartet.
Gemini 7 launches on a two-week mission.
The Indian Navy attacks Karachi in Operation Trident.
Pan Am, once America's greatest airline, ceases operations.
NASA launches Mars Pathfinder.

births.text: Tyra Banks, American model and TV host

facts.text: India's Navy Day remembers Operation Trident, the 1971 missile-boat attack on Karachi harbour.
No one ever discovered what happened to the crew of the Mary Celeste.

12-05.script:
On the fifth of December in 1933, Americans raised their glasses legally for the first time in thirteen years. Prohibition had ended.

On this day in 1945, five navy bombers known as Flight 19 took off from Florida on a training flight. Somewhere over the sea, they lost their way and disappeared, and the legend of the Bermuda Triangle grew.

In 1952, a thick, cold fog settled over London and mixed with the smoke of countless coal fires. For five days, people could barely see their own feet. The Great Smog led to Britain's first clean air laws.

In 1955, the people of Montgomery, Alabama, began to walk. Rather than ride segregated buses, they walked to work, to school and to church, for more than a year.

Born on this day in 1901 was Walt Disney, who dreamed up a mouse and a magic kingdom. And on this day in 2013, Nelson Mandela died, after a long walk to freedom.

Today is International Volunteer Day, and World Soil Day.

events.text: Christopher Columbus reaches the island of Hispaniola.
Auctioneer James Christie holds his first sale in London.
Prohibition ends in the United States.
The Soviet Union adopts a new constitution.
The Soviet army launches its counter-offensive at Moscow.
Flight 19, five U.S. Navy bombers, disappears over the Atlantic.
The Great Smog begins in London.
The Montgomery bus boycott begins.
The Queen makes the first direct-dialled trunk call in Britain, from Bristol to Edinburgh.
Nelson Mandela dies in Johannesburg, aged 95.
NASA's Orion spacecraft makes its first test flight.

births.text: Walt Disney, American animator and film producer
Little Richard, American rock and roll pioneer

facts.text: World Soil Day has been celebrated by the United Nations since 2014.

12-06.script:
Today is Saint Nicholas Day, when children in many countries wake to find small gifts in their shoes.

On the sixth of December in 1917, Finland declared its independence. Finns celebrate quietly, with two candles in every window.

On that same morning in 1917, in the harbour of Halifax in Canada, a ship loaded with explosives caught fire and blew up. It was the largest man-made explosion the world had ever known, and the city was devastated.

In 1877, Thomas Edison leaned towards his new phonograph and recited: Mary had a little lamb. When the machine played his voice back, even he was amazed.

In 1865, the Thirteenth Amendment was ratified, and slavery was abolished across the United States.

In India, today is Mahaparinirvan Diwas, remembering Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, the architect of the Indian Constitution, who passed away on this day in 1956. Millions honour him for a lifetime of fighting for equality.

events.text: The first part of the Encyclopædia Britannica is published in Edinburgh.
The Thirteenth Amendment is ratified, abolishing slavery in the United States.
Thomas Edison makes the first recording of a human voice on his phonograph.
The capstone is set on the Washington Monument, completing it.
The Halifax Explosion devastates the Canadian port city.
Finland declares independence from Russia.
The Irish Free State comes into being.
America's first attempt to launch a satellite, Vanguard TV-3, explodes on the pad.
Gerald Ford is sworn in as Vice President of the United States.
Astronauts join Unity to Zarya, the first two pieces of the International Space Station.

births.text: Charles Martin Hall, American chemist who made aluminium cheap

deaths.text: B. R. Ambedkar, architect of the Constitution of India

12-07.script:
On the morning of the seventh of December in 1941, Japanese planes swept over the American naval base at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. The attack drew the United States into the Second World War. President Roosevelt called it a date which will live in infamy.

On this same date in 1972, the crew of Apollo 17, on their way to the Moon, looked back and took a photograph of the whole Earth, fully lit by the Sun, blue and white and round against the black of space. The Blue Marble became one of the most famous pictures ever taken.

In 1995, a probe dropped from the Galileo spacecraft plunged into the clouds of Jupiter, sending back readings until it was crushed.

In 1988, a terrible earthquake struck Armenia, and the world sent help.

In India, today is Armed Forces Flag Day, honouring those who serve. And born on this day in 1598 was Gian Lorenzo Bernini, whose sculptures seem to breathe.

events.text: Delaware becomes the first state to ratify the U.S. Constitution.
Germany's first railway opens between Nuremberg and Fürth.
The New York Philharmonic gives its first concert.
Japan attacks Pearl Harbor.
West German Chancellor Willy Brandt kneels at the Warsaw Ghetto memorial.
Apollo 17 launches; its crew takes the Blue Marble photograph of Earth.
Indonesia invades East Timor.
An earthquake strikes northern Armenia, killing about 25,000 people.
Mikhail Gorbachev announces large cuts to Soviet forces in a speech at the United Nations.
The Galileo spacecraft arrives at Jupiter and drops a probe into its atmosphere.

facts.text: International Civil Aviation Day marks the signing of the Chicago Convention on 7 December 1944.

12-08.script:
Today some Buddhists celebrate Bodhi Day, remembering the morning the Buddha found enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree.

On the eighth of December in 1941, the United States declared war on Japan, one day after Pearl Harbor.

Twelve years later, on this date in 1953, President Eisenhower stood before the United Nations and spoke of Atoms for Peace, a hope that the power of the atom could light cities instead of destroying them.

In 1987, Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev signed a treaty in Washington, agreeing for the first time to destroy an entire class of nuclear missiles.

And in 1991, leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus met in a forest lodge and signed an agreement that ended the Soviet Union.

But for many, the eighth of December is remembered for a sadder reason. In 1980, outside his home in New York, John Lennon was shot and killed. Fans gathered in Central Park and sang his songs of peace.

Born on this day in 1542 was Mary, Queen of Scots.

events.text: Pope Pius IX proclaims the dogma of the Immaculate Conception.
The Clifton Suspension Bridge opens in Bristol.
The United States declares war on Japan.
Eisenhower gives his "Atoms for Peace" speech at the United Nations.
The Council of Europe adopts the flag of twelve gold stars on blue.
John Lennon is shot and killed in New York.
Reagan and Gorbachev sign the INF Treaty.
The Galileo spacecraft swings past Earth on its way to Jupiter.
The Belovezha Accords declare that the Soviet Union has ceased to exist.
The asteroid Toutatis passes close to Earth and is mapped by radar.
The North American Free Trade Agreement is signed into law.
SpaceX's Dragon becomes the first commercial spacecraft recovered from orbit.

facts.text: On Bodhi Day, Buddhists remember the Buddha's enlightenment under the Bodhi tree.

12-09.script:
On the ninth of December in 1968, in a hall in San Francisco, an engineer named Douglas Engelbart sat at a desk and gave a demonstration that seemed like magic. He used a small wooden box with wheels, a mouse, to point at a screen. He showed windows, links and video calls, decades before most people had ever touched a computer. People still call it the mother of all demos.

On this same date in 1979, scientists certified that smallpox, a disease that had haunted humanity for thousands of years, had been wiped out forever.

In 1946, the Constituent Assembly of India met for the first time in New Delhi, to begin writing the nation's constitution.

In 1961, Tanganyika became independent, and soon joined with Zanzibar to form Tanzania.

And in 1965, a gentle animated special about a boy and a little Christmas tree first aired. A Charlie Brown Christmas has been shown every year since.

Born on this day in 1906 was Grace Hopper, a pioneer of computer programming.

events.text: The Constituent Assembly of India meets for the first time.
The UN adopts the Genocide Convention.
Coronation Street is first broadcast in Britain.
Tanganyika gains independence from the United Kingdom.
A Charlie Brown Christmas is first broadcast.
Douglas Engelbart presents the computer mouse and much more in "the Mother of All Demos".
The Pioneer Venus probes plunge into the atmosphere of Venus.
Smallpox is certified as eradicated.
Lech Wałęsa is elected President of Poland.
Prince Charles and Princess Diana announce their separation.

facts.text: International Anti-Corruption Day marks the signing of the UN Convention against Corruption in 2003.

12-10.script:
Today is Human Rights Day. On the tenth of December in 1948, in Paris, the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Its first article says that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. Eleanor Roosevelt, who guided its writing, called it a Magna Carta for all humankind.

On this day each year, the Nobel Prizes are awarded, on the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death. The very first were given in 1901. Two years later, in 1903, Marie Curie became the first woman to win one, sharing the prize in physics with her husband Pierre.

Born on this day in 1815 was Ada Lovelace, the daughter of the poet Byron. She imagined, long before computers existed, that a machine might one day compose music. And in 1830, the poet Emily Dickinson was born.

In 1868, the world's first traffic light was installed outside the Houses of Parliament in London, lit by gas.

A day for rights, for recognition, and for remarkable minds.

events.text: Mississippi becomes the 20th U.S. state.
The world's first traffic light is installed outside the Houses of Parliament in London.
Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn is first published, in Britain.
The Treaty of Paris ends the Spanish-American War.
The first Nobel Prizes are awarded.
Wilhelm Röntgen receives the first Nobel Prize in Physics, for discovering X-rays.
Marie Curie becomes the first woman to be awarded a Nobel Prize.
King Edward VIII signs his abdication.
The UN adopts the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
Democracy returns to Argentina as Raúl Alfonsín takes office.

births.text: Melvil Dewey, American librarian (Dewey Decimal System)
C. Rajagopalachari, last Governor-General of India
Kenneth Branagh, British actor and director

deaths.text: Alfred Nobel, Swedish chemist and founder of the Nobel Prizes

facts.text: The Nobel Prizes are presented on 10 December because it is the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death in 1896.

12-11.script:
Today is International Mountain Day, a good day to look up.

On the eleventh of December in 1972, the lunar module Challenger settled into a valley on the Moon called Taurus-Littrow. Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt, a geologist, spent three days exploring its hills. They were the last people ever to walk on the Moon.

In 1946, the United Nations created UNICEF to help children whose lives had been torn apart by war. It still works for children in almost every country on Earth.

In 1997, in the city of Kyoto, nations agreed for the first time to cut the gases that warm our planet.

In 1941, Germany declared war on the United States, and the Second World War became truly global.

Born on this day were the composer Hector Berlioz in 1803, the Tamil poet Subramania Bharati in 1882, the writer Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn in 1918, and in 1969, Viswanathan Anand, who became India's first chess grandmaster.

events.text: Indiana becomes the 19th U.S. state.
Dentist Horace Wells has a tooth pulled under laughing gas, pioneering anaesthesia.
General Allenby walks into Jerusalem after the Ottoman surrender.
Edward VIII broadcasts his abdication, giving up the throne "for the woman I love".
Germany and Italy declare war on the United States.
The United Nations creates UNICEF.
Apollo 17 lands on the Moon, the last crewed lunar landing.
Muhammad Ali fights for the last time.
Russian troops enter Chechnya.
The Kyoto Protocol on climate change is adopted.

facts.text: International Mountain Day was first celebrated in 2003, after the UN's International Year of Mountains.

names: Feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe
12-12.script:
On the twelfth of December in 1901, on a windy hill in Newfoundland, Guglielmo Marconi held an earpiece to his ear and listened. Faintly, he heard three clicks: the letter S in Morse code, sent from Cornwall across the Atlantic Ocean. A message had crossed the sea through the air, and the age of radio had arrived.

On this day in 1911, at a magnificent durbar in Delhi, King George the Fifth announced that the capital of British India would move from Calcutta to Delhi.

In 1963, Kenya became independent, and today Kenyans celebrate Jamhuri Day.

In 2015, in Paris, nearly every nation on Earth agreed to work together to keep our planet from warming too much. When the Paris Agreement was adopted, delegates stood and cheered.

Born on this day were Frank Sinatra in 1915, and in 1950, Rajinikanth, whose style made him a legend of Indian cinema.

events.text: Pennsylvania becomes the second state to ratify the U.S. Constitution.
Dentist George Grant patents the wooden golf tee.
Guglielmo Marconi receives the first transatlantic radio signal.
At the Delhi Durbar, King George V announces the capital will move from Calcutta to Delhi.
The first motel opens in San Luis Obispo, California.
Japanese aircraft sink the U.S. gunboat Panay on the Yangtze River.
Kenya gains independence from the United Kingdom.
Zimbabwe Rhodesia returns to British rule ahead of independence as Zimbabwe.
The U.S. Supreme Court's ruling in Bush v. Gore settles the presidential election.
The Paris Agreement on climate change is adopted.

12-13.script:
In Sweden, today is Saint Lucy's Day. Before dawn, girls in white dresses walk in procession with crowns of candles in their hair, bringing light to the darkest time of the year.

On the thirteenth of December in 1577, Francis Drake set sail from Plymouth with five small ships. He would become the first Englishman to sail around the world.

On this day in 1642, the Dutch explorer Abel Tasman became the first European to see the mountains of New Zealand rising from the sea.

In 1928, in New York, an orchestra played a joyful new piece full of honking taxi horns: George Gershwin's An American in Paris.

The thirteenth of December also carries hard memories. In 1937, the Chinese city of Nanjing fell, and terrible suffering followed. In 2001, terrorists attacked India's Parliament, and brave security guards gave their lives to protect it.

Born on this day in 1989 was Taylor Swift, whose songs have become the soundtrack of a generation.

events.text: The Council of Trent opens, launching the Catholic Counter-Reformation.
Francis Drake sets out from Plymouth on his voyage around the world.
Massachusetts organises its first militia regiments, the origin of the U.S. National Guard.
Abel Tasman becomes the first European to sight New Zealand.
George Gershwin's An American in Paris premieres in New York.
Japanese forces capture Nanjing, beginning the Nanjing Massacre.
NASA launches Relay 1, an early communications satellite.
Malta becomes a republic.
Al Gore concedes the U.S. presidential election to George W. Bush.
Terrorists attack the Parliament of India in New Delhi.
Former Iraqi president Saddam Hussein is captured.

births.text: Mary Todd Lincoln, First Lady of the United States

facts.text: On Saint Lucy's Day in Sweden, a girl dressed in white and wearing a crown of candles leads a procession of song.
Under the old Julian calendar, Saint Lucy's Day fell close to the longest night of the year.

12-14.script:
On the fourteenth of December in 1911, after racing across the Antarctic ice with sledges and dogs, the Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen and his four companions reached the South Pole. They planted their flag, and left a tent and a letter for Captain Scott, who arrived five weeks later.

Exactly sixty-one years later, on the fourteenth of December in 1972, Gene Cernan climbed the ladder of his lunar module. He was the last person to stand on the Moon. Before he left, he said: we leave as we came, and, God willing, as we shall return, with peace and hope for all mankind.

In 1900, the physicist Max Planck presented an idea that energy comes in tiny packets. He called them quanta, and quantum physics was born.

In 1962, Mariner 2 flew past Venus, the first successful visit to another planet.

Born on this day in 1924 was Raj Kapoor, the great showman of Indian cinema. And in India, today is National Energy Conservation Day.

events.text: George Washington dies at Mount Vernon.
Alabama becomes the 22nd U.S. state.
The Glasgow Subway, the world's third-oldest underground railway, opens.
Max Planck presents the idea of energy quanta, the start of quantum physics.
Roald Amundsen's expedition becomes the first to reach the South Pole.
Women vote in a British general election for the first time.
The Soviet Union is expelled from the League of Nations.
Mariner 2 flies past Venus, the first successful planetary flyby.
Gene Cernan becomes the last person to walk on the Moon.
Israel extends its law to the Golan Heights.
The Dayton Agreement ending the Bosnian War is signed in Paris.

births.text: George VI, King of the United Kingdom
Raj Kapoor, Indian actor and filmmaker

facts.text: Amundsen's team reached the South Pole about five weeks before Scott's.
Before leaving the Moon, Gene Cernan traced his daughter's initials in the lunar dust.

12-15.script:
Today is International Tea Day, so perhaps put the kettle on.

On the fifteenth of December in 1791, the first ten amendments to the American Constitution, the Bill of Rights, were ratified, protecting freedom of speech, of religion, and of the press.

In 1939, the city of Atlanta threw a grand celebration for the premiere of Gone with the Wind, one of the most famous films ever made.

In 1965, high above the Earth, two Gemini spacecraft drifted to within a few feet of each other. It was the first time two crewed ships had met in space, a skill that would be needed to reach the Moon.

And in 1970, the Soviet probe Venera 7 landed on Venus and, for about twenty minutes, sent back faint signals. It was the first transmission ever received from the surface of another planet.

Born on this day in 1832 was Gustave Eiffel, who built the iron tower that became the symbol of Paris, and in 1859, L. L. Zamenhof, who invented Esperanto, a language he hoped would bring the world together.

events.text: Simon Marius makes the first telescopic observation of the Andromeda Galaxy.
The U.S. Bill of Rights is ratified.
Lakota leader Sitting Bull is killed during an attempt to arrest him.
Gone with the Wind premieres in Atlanta.
Adolf Eichmann is sentenced to death in Jerusalem.
Canada's House of Commons approves the Maple Leaf flag.
Gemini 6A and Gemini 7 make the first crewed rendezvous in space.
Walt Disney dies in Burbank, California.
Venera 7 lands on Venus, the first transmission from another planet's surface.
The Leaning Tower of Pisa reopens after more than a decade of work to stop it falling.

births.text: L. L. Zamenhof, creator of Esperanto
J. Paul Getty, American oil tycoon

deaths.text: Walt Disney, American animator and film producer

facts.text: International Tea Day has been celebrated in tea-producing countries since 2005.
The Eiffel Tower, by Gustave Eiffel (born today), was the world's tallest structure for 41 years.

12-16.script:
On the sixteenth of December in 1971, in Dhaka, the commander of Pakistan's forces in the east signed the instrument of surrender before Indian and Bangladeshi commanders. After nine months of war and terrible suffering, Bangladesh was free. India remembers today as Vijay Diwas, and Bangladesh as Victory Day.

Two centuries earlier, on a cold night in 1773, men disguised as Mohawk warriors boarded ships in Boston Harbor and tipped chests of tea into the sea, protesting a tax they had no say in. The Boston Tea Party pushed the colonies towards revolution.

In 1944, German armies launched a surprise attack through the snowy forests of the Ardennes, beginning the Battle of the Bulge.

In 1811, the first of a series of great earthquakes shook the ground near New Madrid, Missouri. Before they were over, the Mississippi River itself seemed, for a time, to run backwards.

Born on this day were Jane Austen in 1775, and Arthur C. Clarke in 1917, who imagined satellites long before they existed. And around this day in 1770, Ludwig van Beethoven was born.

events.text: Mount Vesuvius erupts violently, its largest eruption in centuries.
Oliver Cromwell becomes Lord Protector of England.
The English Bill of Rights becomes law.
The Boston Tea Party: colonists dump British tea into Boston Harbor.
The first of the great New Madrid earthquakes shakes the Mississippi valley.
The Great Fire of New York destroys much of lower Manhattan.
The Battle of the Bulge begins in the Ardennes.
Scientists at Bell Labs build the first working transistor.
Pakistani forces surrender in Dhaka, and Bangladesh wins its independence.
Kazakhstan declares independence, the last Soviet republic to do so.
Flashing lights in a Pokémon cartoon send hundreds of Japanese children to hospital.

births.text: Ludwig van Beethoven, German composer (baptised 17 December)
Arthur C. Clarke, British science-fiction author

12-17.script:
On the seventeenth of December in 1903, on the windswept sands of Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville Wright lay on the lower wing of a fragile machine of wood and fabric. The engine roared, the Flyer lifted off, and for twelve seconds it flew. His brother Wilbur ran alongside. They flew three more times that day. Humanity had learned to fly.

In 1938, in a laboratory in Berlin, the chemist Otto Hahn found something puzzling: uranium atoms had split in two. Nuclear fission had been discovered.

In 1989, a yellow family from Springfield arrived on television screens in their first full episode. The Simpsons would become the longest-running animated series in history.

In 2010, a young fruit seller in Tunisia named Mohamed Bouazizi, desperate after years of humiliation, set himself on fire. His act sparked the protests known as the Arab Spring.

Today is the National Day of Bhutan, remembering the crowning of its first king in 1907. Born on this day in 1936 was Jorge Mario Bergoglio, who became Pope Francis.

events.text: France recognises the independence of the United States.
The great Aztec Sun Stone is unearthed in Mexico City.
The first issue of Vogue is published.
The Wright brothers make the first powered aeroplane flights at Kitty Hawk.
Ugyen Wangchuck is crowned the first King of Bhutan.
The first NFL Championship Game is played, in Chicago.
Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann discover nuclear fission.
The U.S. Air Force closes Project Blue Book, its study of UFOs.
The Simpsons premieres as a half-hour series.
Mohamed Bouazizi's protest in Tunisia sparks the Arab Spring.

births.text: William Lyon Mackenzie King, Prime Minister of Canada

facts.text: Orville Wright's first flight lasted about 12 seconds and covered 37 metres — less than the wingspan of a jumbo jet.
Humphry Davy, born today, invented a safety lamp that saved countless miners' lives.

12-18.script:
On the eighteenth of December in 1892, in St. Petersburg, the curtain rose on a new ballet by Tchaikovsky. A young girl named Clara received a nutcracker on Christmas Eve, and that night it came alive. The Nutcracker has danced its way into every winter since.

On this day in 1958, America launched a satellite called SCORE, and the next day it broadcast a recorded Christmas message from President Eisenhower down to the Earth. It was the first time a human voice had been sent from space.

In 1961, Indian forces moved into Goa, and within two days more than four centuries of Portuguese rule came to an end.

In 1898, a French count drove an electric car at about sixty-three kilometres an hour, setting the world's first land speed record.

Today is International Migrants Day, honouring everyone who has made a home far from where they were born. It is also Qatar's National Day, and Arabic Language Day. Born on this day in 1946 was Steven Spielberg, who has shown us dinosaurs, aliens and heroes.

events.text: The United States celebrates its first Thanksgiving, marking the victory at Saratoga.
Jassim bin Mohammed Al Thani becomes ruler of Qatar, the date of its National Day.
Tchaikovsky's ballet The Nutcracker premieres in St. Petersburg.
Gaston de Chasseloup-Laubat sets the first land speed record in an electric car.
The "Piltdown Man" fossil, later exposed as a hoax, is announced in London.
The Battle of Verdun ends after ten months of fighting.
Project SCORE, the first communications satellite, is launched.
Indian forces enter Goa, ending Portuguese rule.
Britain abolishes the death penalty for murder permanently.
Argentina win the World Cup in Qatar, beating France on penalties.

12-19.script:
On the nineteenth of December in 1843, in London, a slim little book with a red cover went on sale in time for Christmas. Charles Dickens had written it in just six weeks. A Christmas Carol told of a mean old miser named Ebenezer Scrooge, visited by three ghosts, who wakes on Christmas morning a changed man. The first copies sold out within days.

On this day in 1961, Goa became part of India after four and a half centuries of Portuguese rule. Goa celebrates today as Liberation Day.

In 1972, the capsule of Apollo 17 splashed down in the Pacific. It was the end of the last journey to the Moon, and no one has been back since.

In 1984, Britain and China signed an agreement to return Hong Kong to China in 1997.

And in 1997, a film about a great ship and a love story aboard it was released. Titanic would become one of the most successful films ever made.

Born on this day in 1915 was Édith Piaf, the little sparrow of Paris, who sang that she regretted nothing.

events.text: Benjamin Franklin publishes the first Poor Richard's Almanack.
Charles Dickens publishes A Christmas Carol.
Adolf Hitler takes personal command of the German army.
Project SCORE broadcasts President Eisenhower's Christmas message from orbit.
Goa is liberated from Portuguese rule and joins India.
Apollo 17 returns to Earth, ending the last crewed Moon mission.
Britain and China sign the Joint Declaration on the future of Hong Kong.
The film Titanic is released.
The U.S. House of Representatives impeaches President Bill Clinton.
The European Space Agency launches Gaia to map a billion stars.

births.text: Carter G. Woodson, American historian, "father of Black history"
Pratibha Patil, first woman President of India

facts.text: Dickens published A Christmas Carol at his own expense, and the first printing sold out by Christmas Eve.
Titanic, released today in 1997, became the first film to earn more than a billion dollars.

12-20.script:
On the twentieth of December in 1803, in New Orleans, the French flag came down and the American flag went up. With the Louisiana Purchase, the young United States had doubled in size overnight.

On this same date in 1951, at a quiet test station in the Idaho desert, scientists switched on a small experimental reactor. Its heat lit four ordinary light bulbs. It was the first time electricity had ever been made from nuclear power.

In 1946, a film about a man who thinks his life has been worthless, until an angel shows him what the world would be like without him, opened in New York. It's a Wonderful Life is now watched every Christmas.

In 1860, South Carolina became the first state to leave the Union, and the road to civil war grew shorter.

And in 1999, Portugal handed Macau back to China, ending more than four centuries of European rule in Asia.

Today is International Human Solidarity Day. Born on this day in 1901 was Robert Van de Graaff, who built the generator that makes your hair stand on end.

events.text: Richard the Lionheart is captured in Austria on his way home from the Crusade.
Three ships sail from London carrying the settlers who will found Jamestown, Virginia.
Peter the Great orders Russia to start its new year on 1 January.
The Louisiana Purchase is completed in New Orleans.
South Carolina becomes the first state to secede from the Union.
Electric arc lights illuminate a stretch of Broadway in New York.
It's a Wonderful Life premieres in New York.
EBR-I in Idaho becomes the first nuclear reactor to generate electricity.
Elvis Presley receives his draft notice for the U.S. Army.
The first production Boeing 707 makes its maiden flight.
The United States invades Panama.
Portugal hands Macau over to China.

births.text: Robert Menzies, Prime Minister of Australia
Robert J. Van de Graaff, American physicist

facts.text: International Human Solidarity Day was declared by the United Nations in 2005.

12-21.script:
Today, in the northern half of the world, is the winter solstice, the shortest day and the longest night. Since ancient times, people have lit fires and gathered close, knowing that tomorrow the light begins to return. In Iran, families stay up late on Yalda Night, eating pomegranates and reading poetry.

On the twenty-first of December in 1968, three astronauts climbed into Apollo 8 and rode a Saturn V rocket away from the Earth. They would be the first people ever to leave our planet behind and travel to the Moon.

In 1891, in a gymnasium in Massachusetts, a teacher named James Naismith nailed two peach baskets to a balcony and invented a game to keep his students busy indoors. Basketball was born.

In 1913, a newspaper in New York printed a puzzle shaped like a diamond, with clues that crossed. It was the first crossword.

In 1937, Walt Disney's Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs premiered, the first full-length animated feature film in English.

Today is also World Meditation Day. A good night for stillness, and for the quiet promise of the returning light.

events.text: The Pilgrims land at Plymouth, Massachusetts.
James Naismith's students play the first game of basketball.
The first crossword puzzle is published in the New York World.
Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs premieres.
Charles de Gaulle is elected President of France.
Apollo 8 launches, carrying the first humans towards the Moon.
Pan Am Flight 103 is destroyed by a bomb over Lockerbie, Scotland.
The Antonov An-225, the heaviest aircraft ever built, makes its first flight.
Eleven former Soviet republics form the Commonwealth of Independent States.
Jupiter and Saturn appear closer in the sky than at any time in nearly 400 years.

12-22.script:
On the twenty-second of December in 1887, in the town of Erode in southern India, a boy named Srinivasa Ramanujan was born. With almost no formal training, he filled notebooks with astonishing formulas that still amaze mathematicians today. India celebrates his birthday as National Mathematics Day.

On this day in 1938, a museum curator in South Africa named Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer looked at a strange blue fish brought in by a fishing boat. It was a coelacanth, a fish believed to have died out with the dinosaurs, alive and well after all.

In 1882, in New York, Thomas Edison's partner Edward Johnson wired eighty little red, white and blue electric bulbs around a Christmas tree. It was the first electrically lit Christmas tree.

And in 1989, the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin opened again after twenty-eight years. In Romania that same day, the people rose up and the dictator Ceaușescu fled.

Born on this day in 1858 was Giacomo Puccini, whose operas still bring audiences to tears.

events.text: The U.S. Congress passes the Embargo Act, banning trade with foreign nations.
Fyodor Dostoevsky faces a mock execution in St. Petersburg before his sentence is commuted.
Edward Johnson displays the first electrically lit Christmas tree.
Alfred Dreyfus is wrongly convicted of treason in France.
A living coelacanth, a fish thought extinct, is identified in South Africa.
Colo becomes the first gorilla born in a zoo, at Columbus, Ohio.
The SR-71 Blackbird, the fastest jet aircraft ever built, makes its first flight.
A 70 mph speed limit is introduced on Britain's roads.
The Brandenburg Gate in Berlin reopens.
Romania's dictator Nicolae Ceaușescu flees as the revolution triumphs.

births.text: Lady Bird Johnson, First Lady of the United States
Maurice and Robin Gibb, British singers (Bee Gees)

facts.text: India's National Mathematics Day honours Srinivasa Ramanujan, born on this day in 1887.
The coelacanth was thought to have died out with the dinosaurs, about 66 million years ago.

12-23.script:
On the twenty-third of December in 1947, at Bell Laboratories in New Jersey, a small group of scientists showed their bosses a little device made of germanium, gold foil and a paper clip. It could amplify a signal, like a vacuum tube, but far smaller. The transistor had been born, and every computer and phone today is built from billions of them.

On this day in 1823, a newspaper in New York published an anonymous poem that began: 'Twas the night before Christmas, when all through the house, not a creature was stirring, not even a mouse. It shaped how the world imagines Santa Claus.

In 1783, George Washington appeared before Congress and resigned his command of the army. He could have ruled; instead he went home to his farm. King George is said to have called him the greatest man in the world.

In 1986, the little Voyager aircraft landed in California after flying all the way around the world without stopping or refuelling.

In India, today is Kisan Diwas, Farmers' Day, the birthday of Chaudhary Charan Singh. Born on this day in 1790 was Jean-François Champollion, who would decipher the Rosetta Stone.

events.text: George Washington resigns as commander-in-chief of the Continental Army.
"A Visit from St. Nicholas" ('Twas the Night Before Christmas) is first published.
Vincent van Gogh cuts off part of his left ear.
The U.S. Federal Reserve is created.
Wake Island falls to Japanese forces.
The transistor is demonstrated at Bell Labs.
Former Japanese Prime Minister Hideki Tojo is executed for war crimes.
Joseph Murray performs the first successful kidney transplant, between identical twins in Boston.
Sixteen survivors of the Andes plane crash are rescued after 72 days.
The Voyager aircraft completes the first non-stop, unrefuelled flight around the world.

births.text: Jean-François Champollion, French decipherer of hieroglyphs
Joseph Smith, American founder of the Latter Day Saint movement
Charan Singh, Prime Minister of India

Champollion, born today, cracked Egyptian hieroglyphs with the help of the Rosetta Stone.

12-24.script:
On Christmas Eve in 1818, in the little Austrian village of Oberndorf, the church organ had broken. So the priest, Joseph Mohr, and the schoolteacher, Franz Gruber, sang a new song to the gentle strumming of a guitar. It was called Silent Night, and it has been sung on this night ever since, in hundreds of languages.

In 1906, wireless operators on ships at sea were startled to hear, instead of Morse code, a human voice. Reginald Fessenden played the violin and read from the Bible, perhaps the first radio broadcast of voice and music.

And on Christmas Eve in 1968, the crew of Apollo 8 became the first humans to orbit the Moon. As the Earth rose over the lunar horizon, they photographed it, a blue and white jewel in the darkness. That night, they read from the Book of Genesis to the largest audience in history, and wished everyone on the good Earth a merry Christmas.

In 1814, the Treaty of Ghent ended the War of 1812, and in 1951, Libya became independent.

Born on this day in 1924 was Mohammed Rafi, whose voice still fills Indian hearts with song.

events.text: The Treaty of Ghent ends the War of 1812.
"Silent Night" is performed for the first time, in Oberndorf, Austria.
Verdi's opera Aida premieres in Cairo.
Reginald Fessenden makes what may be the first radio broadcast of voice and music.
The first National Christmas Tree is lit at the White House.
Libya gains independence.
The U.S. military's tradition of "tracking" Santa's sleigh begins, after a misprinted phone number in a newspaper advert.
Apollo 8 orbits the Moon and photographs Earthrise.
Europe's first Ariane rocket is launched.
The Soviet Union begins its invasion of Afghanistan.

births.text: Howard Hughes, American aviator and film producer

12-25.script:
On Christmas Day in 1914, along the frozen trenches of the Western Front, something extraordinary happened. British and German soldiers who had been fighting each other climbed out, shook hands in no man's land, swapped chocolate and cigarettes, sang carols, and in some places even played football. For a few hours, the war stopped.

Many crowns have been placed on Christmas Day. In the year 800, in Rome, the Pope crowned Charlemagne emperor. In 1066, William the Conqueror was crowned King of England in Westminster Abbey.

On Christmas night in 1758, a farmer and amateur astronomer in Germany saw a comet appear in the sky, exactly as Edmond Halley had predicted, long after his death.

In 1991, Mikhail Gorbachev resigned, and the red flag of the Soviet Union was lowered over the Kremlin for the last time.

And in 2021, the James Webb Space Telescope rose into the sky, to look back at the very first galaxies.

Born on this day were Isaac Newton in 1642, Muhammad Ali Jinnah in 1876, and Atal Bihari Vajpayee in 1924, whose birthday India celebrates as Good Governance Day.

events.text: Charlemagne is crowned Emperor of the Romans in Rome.
William the Conqueror is crowned King of England.

Muhammad Ali Jinnah, founder of Pakistan

12-26.script:
On the twenty-sixth of December in 1898, in Paris, Marie and Pierre Curie announced the discovery of a new element that glowed faintly in the dark. They named it radium, from the Latin word for ray.

On this day in 1776, after crossing the icy Delaware River in the night, George Washington's army surprised the Hessian troops at Trenton. It was a small battle, but it gave a struggling revolution new hope.

In 1966, the first Kwanzaa was celebrated, a week-long festival honouring African heritage, family and community.

The twenty-sixth of December also brings a deep sorrow. In 2004, a great earthquake beneath the Indian Ocean sent waves crashing onto the shores of more than a dozen countries. Around the world, people opened their hearts to help.

In Britain and many other countries, today is Boxing Day. In India, it is Veer Bal Diwas, honouring the courage of the young sons of Guru Gobind Singh.

Born on this day in 1791 was Charles Babbage, who designed the first mechanical computer.

events.text: Washington's army wins the Battle of Trenton.
James Nason patents the coffee percolator.
Marie and Pierre Curie announce the discovery of radium.

births.text: Jared Leto, American actor and singer

12-27.script:
On the twenty-seventh of December in 1831, a small ship called the Beagle sailed out of Plymouth on a voyage around the world. On board was a twenty-two-year-old naturalist named Charles Darwin. The five years ahead would change his life, and our understanding of life itself.

On this day in 1904, in London, a boy who would never grow up flew onto the stage for the first time. Peter Pan asked the audience to clap if they believed in fairies, and they did.

In 1911, at a session of the Indian National Congress in Calcutta, a song written by Rabindranath Tagore was sung for the first time. Jana Gana Mana would become India's national anthem.

In 1968, Apollo 8 splashed down safely in the Pacific, after its crew became the first to see the far side of the Moon with their own eyes.

The day also holds sorrow. In 2007, Benazir Bhutto was assassinated in Pakistan.

Born on this day were Johannes Kepler in 1571, who discovered how the planets move, and Louis Pasteur in 1822, whose work has saved countless lives.

events.text: Charles Darwin sets sail on HMS Beagle.
J. M. Barrie's Peter Pan premieres in London.
"Jana Gana Mana", later India's national anthem, is sung for the first time.
Radio City Music Hall opens in New York.
The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank are founded.
The Netherlands formally recognises Indonesia's independence.

facts.text: Louis Pasteur, born today, developed pasteurisation and early vaccines against rabies and anthrax.
Johannes Kepler, born today, discovered that planets move in ellipses, not circles.
Peter Pan, which premiered on this day, made Wendy a popular girl's name.

12-28.script:
On the twenty-eighth of December in 1895, in the basement of a café in Paris, about thirty people paid one franc each to watch something new. The Lumière brothers switched on their machine, and moving pictures flickered onto a screen: workers leaving a factory, a baby being fed, a gardener getting soaked with a hose. It was the first public film screening, and cinema was born.

On this day in 1612, Galileo, peering through his telescope, noted a faint star near Jupiter. He had actually seen the planet Neptune, more than two centuries before it was discovered.

In 1885, in Bombay, seventy-two delegates met for the first session of the Indian National Congress, which would one day lead the struggle for India's freedom.

In 1973, the United States passed the Endangered Species Act, promising to protect the plants and animals in danger of disappearing.

Born on this day were Dhirubhai Ambani in 1932 and Ratan Tata in 1937, two of India's great builders of industry, and in 1954, the actor Denzel Washington.

events.text: Galileo observes Neptune, without realising it is a planet.
Spain recognises the independence of Mexico.
Iowa becomes the 29th U.S. state.
William Semple patents a chewing gum in the United States.
The Indian National Congress holds its first session in Bombay.

Constance Markievicz becomes the first woman elected to the British House of Commons.
Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn's The Gulag Archipelago is published in Paris.

births.text: Linus Torvalds, Finnish creator of Linux

facts.text: The Lumière brothers' first public show included a film of workers leaving their factory.
Galileo noted Neptune in his notebooks more than 230 years before it was officially discovered.

12-29.script:
On the twenty-ninth of December in 1170, four knights burst into Canterbury Cathedral and killed the Archbishop, Thomas Becket, at the altar. The shock was felt across Europe, and his tomb became a place of pilgrimage for centuries.

On this day in 1959, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a playful lecture to a room of scientists in California. There's plenty of room at the bottom, he told them, imagining machines so small they could write an entire encyclopedia on the head of a pin. It is often seen as the beginning of nanotechnology.

In 1940, German bombs set much of the City of London on fire. The next morning, a famous photograph showed the dome of Saint Paul's Cathedral standing unbroken above the smoke.

And in 1989, the playwright Václav Havel, who had been imprisoned for speaking freely, was elected President of Czechoslovakia.

In 1890, at Wounded Knee in South Dakota, hundreds of Lakota men, women and children were killed by U.S. soldiers, a tragedy still mourned today.

Born on this day in 1942 was Rajesh Khanna, the first superstar of Indian cinema.

events.text: Thomas Becket is murdered in Canterbury Cathedral.
Texas becomes the 28th U.S. state.
The first YMCA in the United States opens in Boston.
U.S. soldiers kill hundreds of Lakota people at Wounded Knee.
Sun Yat-sen is elected provisional President of the Republic of China.

Richard Feynman gives his lecture "There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom".

Václav Havel is elected President of Czechoslovakia.

births.text: Charles Goodyear, American inventor of vulcanised rubber

facts.text: Charles Goodyear, born today, discovered how to vulcanise rubber, reportedly after spilling a mixture on a hot stove.
Feynman's lecture "There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom" is often called the birth of nanotechnology.
Thomas Becket was made a saint just over two years after his murder.

12-30.script:
On the thirtieth of December in 1896, in Manila, the writer and doctor José Rizal walked calmly to his execution. His novels had awakened the Filipino people to the injustice of colonial rule. The night before, he wrote a farewell poem to his beloved country. The Philippines honours him today, on Rizal Day.

On this day in 1943, in Port Blair in the Andaman Islands, Subhas Chandra Bose raised the Indian flag, one of the first times it flew over Indian soil freed from British rule.

In 1922, delegates in Moscow signed a treaty that created the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics.

And in 1916, the mysterious monk Rasputin, who held great influence over Russia's royal family, was killed by a group of nobles in Petrograd.

Born on this day in 1865 was Rudyard Kipling, who gave us The Jungle Book, and in 1879, the sage Ramana Maharshi, who taught that the deepest question is simply: who am I?

events.text: The Gadsden Purchase is agreed between the United States and Mexico.
José Rizal is executed in Manila, inspiring the Philippine Revolution.
Grigori Rasputin is murdered in Petrograd.
The Soviet Union is created.
Tokyo's Ginza Line opens, the first underground railway in Asia.
Workers begin the Flint sit-down strike at General Motors.
Subhas Chandra Bose raises the Indian flag at Port Blair.
The first colour television sets go on sale in the United States.

Israel and the Holy See agree to establish diplomatic relations.
The Cassini spacecraft makes its closest flyby of Jupiter on the way to Saturn.

births.text: Rudyard Kipling, English author of The Jungle Book

facts.text: Rizal Day honours José Rizal, whose novels inspired the Philippine fight for independence.
Rudyard Kipling, born today in Bombay, was the youngest person to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.

12-31.script:
On the last night of the year, the world counts down together, from the islands of the Pacific, through Asia and Europe, to the Americas, welcoming the new year one time zone at a time.

On the thirty-first of December in 1879, crowds took special trains to Menlo Park in New Jersey to see Thomas Edison's new electric lights glowing in the winter night.

In 1907, a ball of iron, wood and light bulbs was lowered down a pole above Times Square in New York for the first time, to mark the new year. People have gathered to watch it ever since.

In 1600, Queen Elizabeth the First granted a charter to a company of merchants trading with the East Indies. The East India Company would change the history of India forever.

And on the banks of the Ravi River in Lahore, on the last night of 1929, Jawaharlal Nehru raised the flag of India and the Congress declared its goal of complete independence.

In 1999, the United States handed the Panama Canal to Panama, and at midnight the world welcomed a new millennium.

Born on this day in 1869 was Henri Matisse, who painted with joyful colour. As the year turns, may your own story be full of colour too. Until our next journey through time.

events.text: Queen Elizabeth I charters the East India Company.
Queen Victoria chooses Ottawa as the capital of Canada.
Thomas Edison demonstrates electric lighting to the public at Menlo Park.
The first New Year's Eve ball drop takes place in Times Square.

Czechoslovakia is peacefully dissolved at midnight.
The United States hands control of the Panama Canal to Panama.
Boris Yeltsin resigns, making Vladimir Putin Russia's acting president.

facts.text: At Hogmanay, "first-footing" says the first guest across the threshold after midnight brings luck for the year.
